explain.headline: Beyond the CJI: What Independence Should Mean for Election Commission Appointments
static: Article 324 of the Constitution provides for the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to be vested in an Election Commission.

Article 324(2) states that the Election Commission shall consist of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners, if any, as the President may from time to time fix.
Appointments of the CEC and ECs are made by the President, subject to the provisions of any law made in that behalf by Parliament.

Historically, before the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act of 2023, ECs were appointed directly by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers.

The Supreme Court in Anoop Baranwal v Union of India (2023) ruled that appointments should be made by the President on the advice of a committee comprising the PM, LoP, and the CJI, pending legislation by Parliament.
explain.what: The article examines the constitutional debate surrounding the appointment process of Election Commissioners under the 2023 Act, questioning whether executive dominance in the selection committee compromises institutional neutrality.
explain.why_in_news: The issue is in the news due to a split verdict by the Supreme Court in Dr Jaya Thakur v Union of India, which challenges the 2023 Act and has referred the matter to a Constitution bench.
explain.background: Article 324 empowers the President to appoint Election Commissioners subject to parliamentary legislation, a legislative gap that existed for decades until the Supreme Court intervened in Anoop Baranwal and Parliament subsequently enacted the 2023 law.
significance: It addresses the foundational constitutional question of institutional autonomy for the Election Commission of India.
It evaluates the balance of power between the executive and the opposition in high-level statutory appointments.
It highlights the difference between judicial interim arrangements and durable parliamentary legislations.
prelims: The 2023 Act being challenged is the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
Section 7 of the 2023 Act places the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, and a Union Cabinet minister on the selection committee.
The Supreme Court case challenging the 2023 Act is Dr Jaya Thakur v Union of India.
Earlier landmark judgments mentioned include Anoop Baranwal v Union of India and T N Seshan v Union of India.
explain.mains: Examine the constitutional debates surrounding the appointment mechanism of Election Commissioners. To what extent does institutional independence depend on selection arithmetic rather than tenure and removal safeguards? (15 Marks, 250 Words)

points: The Supreme Court split in Dr Jaya Thakur v Union of India challenges Section 7 of the 2023 Act, which places the PM, LoP, and a Union Cabinet minister on the EC selection committee.
Justice Dipankar Datta noted the LoP could become ornamental, while Justice Satish Chandra Sharma referred the constitutional question to a larger bench.
The 2023 Act replaced the temporary selection committee setup by the Anoop Baranwal judgment, which included the CJI, the Prime Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition.
The Anoop Baranwal judgment did not hold that the CJI must permanently occupy the third seat or that Parliament could never give the government a numerical majority.
The core issue is whether the government's assured voting power in the selection committee is compatible with the neutrality expected of the election watchdog.
Past cases like T N Seshan v Union of India caution against equating a numerical majority within the Commission with executive capture, citing independent conduct by appointed members.
Indian laws use various appointment models, such as the Central Vigilance Commissioner and Chief Information Commissioner panels where two of three members belong to the government.
Conversely, the CBI Director is selected by a committee comprising the PM, LoP, and the CJI or a nominated Supreme Court judge.
The upcoming Constitution bench must formulate a durable principle to define the minimum non-government safeguard that Parliament must preserve under Article 324.
sum.text:
In June 1949, B R Ambedkar told the Constituent Assembly that the method of appointing election commissioners had given him “a great deal of headache”.
Security of tenure, he said, would mean little if the Constitution could not prevent the appointment of “a fool or a knave or a person who is likely to be under the thumb of the Executive”.
Nearly eight decades later, the headache has returned: how far must the appointment process be insulated from the government of the day?
That issue underlies the Supreme Court’s September 23 split in Dr Jaya Thakur v Union of India, which challenges the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. Section 7 places the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition (LoP), and a Union Cabinet minister nominated by the Prime Minister on the selection committee. When the two government members agree, the Opposition member cannot prevent their choice from prevailing.
Justice Dipankar Datta observed that the LoP could consequently become “largely ornamental”, while Justice Satish Chandra Sharma considered the resulting constitutional issue one that Anoop Baranwal v Union of India had not answered.
Their disagreement over Article 145(3) has receded in practical importance because both asked the Chief Justice of India (CJI) to consider constituting a Constitution bench, placing the substantive issue before a larger bench.
Anoop Baranwal confronted a system in which ECs were appointed based on executive advice because Parliament had never enacted the law contemplated by Article 324(2).
The five-judge bench prescribed a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the LoP, and the CJI, expressly as a temporary arrangement until Parliament legislated. Its reasoning repeatedly addressed appointments remaining in the “sole” or “exclusive” hands of the executive, without holding that the CJI must permanently occupy the third seat or that Parliament could never give the government a numerical majority.
Because neither proposition was decided, an important gap remains: it takes no constitutional interpretation to see that two votes defeat one and that the government can carry the selection without the Opposition member’s concurrence.
What requires five judges is deciding whether that assured voting power is compatible with the neutrality and independence expected of the constitutional body supervising elections in which the incumbent government is itself a…

stories.summary: Apple Pay was launched in India after significant regulatory developments by the Reserve Bank of India. This new payment option allows users to pay securely without needing an OTP, which can facilitate fraud. The RBI has shifted towards regulating outcomes rather than prescribing specific technologies for digital payments. While Apple Pay currently does not support RuPay or UPI, it shows how regulation can foster innovation.

explain.headline: Apple Pay Launch in India Highlights RBI's Outcome-Based Regulation
static: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is India's central banking institution established on April 1, 1935, under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, responsible for regulating the monetary policy and payment systems.

The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) is an umbrella organisation for operating retail payments and settlement systems in India, created by RBI and the Indian Banks' Association under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.

Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) in India includes foundational identity (Aadhaar), fast payment rails (UPI), document wallets (DigiLocker), consent frameworks (Account Aggregator), and open commerce (ONDC).

Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) is a security process where a user provides two different authentication factors to verify themselves, widely mandated by RBI for digital transactions to prevent fraud.
explain.what: Apple Pay launched in India on September 30, enabled by RBI's new outcome-based regulatory framework that permits device-native biometrics instead of mandatory OTPs for card payments.
explain.why_in_news: Apple Pay arrived in India after the RBI issued its Authentication Mechanisms for Digital Payment Transactions Directions.
explain.background: RBI shifted from mandating specific authentication technologies like OTPs to regulating outcomes and principles, enabling flexible authentication methods like device biometrics.
significance: Demonstrates the effectiveness of outcome-based regulation in fostering technological innovation in digital payments.
Addresses security vulnerabilities associated with OTP-based fraud while reducing payment friction.

Yemen's long war has flared again , this time as a spillover of the US-Iran conflict. Fighting along the Red Sea coast has intensified as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces seek to secure the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, through which roughly 12 per cent of global maritime trade passes, while the Iran-backed Houthis have struck Saudi airports and oil facilities. With traffic through the Strait of Hormuz restricted, the Red Sea route matters more for energy exports, raising the stakes well beyond Yemen. But it is the Yemeni people, worn down by more than a decade of war, who will continue to suffer the most.
The 2022 UN-brokered truce largely froze the fighting and gave the Houthis, classified as a terrorist outfit by the US and several other countries, time to regroup. They subsequently began targeting ships linked to Israel in the Red Sea amid the Gaza war. US and British strikes in 2024, followed by a sustained US bombing campaign in 2025, failed to defeat them; neither did the Israeli strikes on Houthi-controlled ports. The fragile truce shattered in July. The conflicts in Iran and Yemen are now intertwined. Escalation in Yemen suits Tehran, which can use the Houthis to gain leverage over the region's chokepoints. A sustained war would also complicate a US-Iran settlement. A political resolution between the Houthis and the Yemeni government looks distant, but the alternative -- another prolonged military campaign -- would be far worse.
The Yemen war is also the first real test of the Mecca Pact. Neither Turkey nor Pakistan has shown much appetite to be part of an anti-Houthi offensive. After the alliance’s emergency meeting in Riyadh this week, Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistan and Turkey had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were engaged in combat. Islamabad knows that offensive support would cross Tehran’s red lines. Thus, the pact may offer Riyadh some political backing, but it is unlikely to deter the Houthis. As the last few years have shown, military force can impose costs, but cannot by itself neutralise the group or resolve the long-running conflict.

KOCHI: The Kerala High Court on Friday directed the State Police Chief to register an FIR against former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, his daughter Veena T, and her husband, former minister P A Mohammad Riyas, in the CMRL-Exalogic pay-off case . ED's counsel pointed out that during the investigation, which related to a scheduled offence under the PMLA, the ED found materials indicating the commission of an offence that could attract provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The ED submitted that Section 66(2) of the PMLA, read with the Supreme Court's judgment in the Lalita Kumari case, makes registration of an FIR obligatory if the information discloses a cognisable offence. One of the most important risks involves cryptography. The Rajya Sabha on Tuesday passed the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026 by a voice vote amid continuous sloganeering and protests by Opposition members. The Bill had already been approved by the Lok Sabha on July 31.
The House passed the legislation after it reassembled at 2 p.m., when Deputy Chairman Harivansh Narayan Singh called upon Minister of State for Home Affairs Nityanand Rai to move the motion for consideration of the Bill. Following its passage, the Rajya Sabha was adjourned till Wednesday.
The amendment introduces a stricter two-tier mechanism for delayed registration of births and deaths under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969.
Under the proposed changes, registrations delayed between one and two years will continue to require approval from the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate or an authorised Executive Magistrate. However, in cases where registration is delayed by more than two years, approval will now be granted only by a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.
The government has said the change shifts the authority for very late registrations from the executive to the judiciary to curb fraudulent records and improve the accuracy and reliability of the country’s civil registration and population database.
Meanwhile, the Lok Sabha passed the Appropriation (No. 3) Bill, 2026 by a voice vote amid protests from Opposition members. The Bill authorises expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India towards excess spending on certain services during the financial year ending March 31, 2023, in excess of the amounts originally authorized for those services.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman also introduced the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill for consideration. The proposed legislation seeks to amend the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, the Income-tax Act, 2025, and the Finance Act, 2026.
The Lok Sabha was later adjourned for the day amid persistent disruptions and will reconvene on Wednesday at 11 a.m.
Both Houses of Parliament witnessed repeated adjournments during the day as Opposition members staged protests over several issues, including alleged irregularities in Ram Mandir donations, police action against protesters during the Parliament March on July 20, and the Cauvery water dispute.
Earlier on Monday, the Lok Sabha had passed a Bill increasing the sanctioned strength of judges in the Supreme Court without discussion amid Opposition protests.
